title: The Punjabi Suba campaign
hookLine: years of peaceful campaigning for a Punjabi-language state

cards: A line of volunteers walks out of a gurdwara, singing, toward the police. They carry no weapons, only a slogan. The police arrest them, and the next day another line walks out, and the day after that another.

The jails fill. The singing goes on. What they want sounds almost ordinary: a state where the language people speak at home, Punjabi, is the language of the schools, the courts and the government offices.
The word for a state or province is suba.

teach.b: First, the ask. After independence, India began redrawing its states around the languages people spoke. Punjab was left as it was, a mix of Punjabi speakers and Hindi speakers.
The Akali Dal, a Sikh political party, asked for a state shaped around Punjabi, written in Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib. Second, the way it was asked.
Leaders like Master Tara Singh and later Sant Fateh Singh led morchas, peaceful campaigns where volunteers marched, courted arrest and went to jail by choice. There were fasts, and promises to fast.
It was the same method this path met at Guru ka Bagh and in the gurdwara reform: no striking back, and no going away. Third, the other side. Not everyone wanted it.

teach.h: SOME FEARED A STATE OF ONE FAITH.
teach.b: Some in Delhi worried that a state drawn around Punjabi would really be a state drawn around religion.
Some Punjabi Hindus said their language was Hindi, and the question of language got tangled up with the question of faith. The campaign was asking a hard question in a crowded room. Fourth, the root.

teach.h: LISTEN A LITTLE, SPEAK A LITTLE.
teach.b: At Ang 661 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that as long as we live in this world, we should listen a little and speak a little. A fair ask does both.
It keeps speaking, and it keeps listening, even when the answer is no, and no again.

how: Sikhs remember the Punjabi Suba campaign as a peaceful political movement led by the Akali Dal; its morchas, with volunteers courting arrest, are told in histories of modern Punjab.

games.why: the campaign kept coming back with marches, arrests and fasts. it kept asking, and kept the method peaceful.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've asked for and been refused, by a parent, a boss, a landlord, a friend.

Breathe in and say the ask to yourself plainly, in one sentence, with no blame in it; breathe out and hear their reason for no as fairly as you can, then ask again, and listen again. If you pray, rest on Waheguru between the two.

wordCard.voice: Punjabi Suba. A state shaped around the Punjabi language, the long, peaceful ask carried on through marches, arrests and fasts. Today's word.

orig.note: a Punjabi state; suba means a state or province.

carryVoice: Your line: ask, and ask again. Speak a little, listen a little, and keep asking. Until tomorrow.
